# Introduction

The CT_prediction_set data set contains data about Conneticut State Police traffic stops. The data ranges from October 2013 to March 2015 and contains roughly 270,000 rows of traffic stops. The data contains 24 variables. The purpose of this project is to determine the outcome of a traffic stop based on the predictor variables. In this RMD, the beginning code cleans the data by removing redundant, uni-variate, and unhelpful predictors. The next two chunks of code address missing variables and data leakage. The following section of code looks into relationships between predictors. This section uses the cleaned data to look at the relationships because in the original data there are a handful of repeat predictors that are almost identical. The final code chunk creates graphs to explore predictors and their responses.

The goal of this project is to build a logistic regression model to predict whether or not a contraband is found. This project will also discuss racial discrimination using the "outcome test." If officers do not discriminate the rate at which they find drugs should be the same across racial groups. If officers unfairly target a racial group for searches, they may conduct more searches of drivers in that group without finding any drugs. This means certain racial groups may have a lower proportion of being searched and the cops actually finding contraband.

# Reading in the Data

```{r, warning = FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(readr)
Stops <- read_csv("CT_Stops.csv")
```

# 3. Exploratory Data Analysis

#### Removing Redundant, Uni-variate, and Unhelpful Predictors

There are 50,000 observations and 22 predictor variables in the data set. We will start by removing `id` , `police department`, and `state` as predictors. Every stop is made by the State Police in Conneticut and stop id is essentially a row number. At a first glance, it seems `driver_age_raw` and `driver_age` are the same, so we will join these two columns. And since `driver_age_raw` has no missing values, we will keep `driver_age_raw`. The same can be said for `driver_race_raw` v. `driver_race`, `violation_raw` v. `violation`, `search_type_raw` v. `search_type`, and `county_name` v. `county_fips`. `county_fips` is just a numeric id for each county.

```{r, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
# Using library dplyr to append
library(dplyr)

# Count missing values for each individual column
COL_NA <- colSums(is.na(Stops))
print(COL_NA)

# Removing the Redundant, Uni-variate, Unhelpful Predictor, and Predictors that leak data
Stops <- Stops %>%
  select(-id, -state, -police_department, -driver_age, -driver_race, -violation, -search_type, -county_fips)
```

#### Missing Variables

-   `stop_time` Since we have a handful of missing values in the `stop_time` predictor, we will impute these. We will take each observation without a `stop_time` value, and look at it's `stop_date` . We will then take the mean `stop_time` from each date and impute any missing values by the mean `stop_time` on that date.

-   `search_type_raw` Over 98% of our observations in `search_type_raw` are NA. This is because over 98% of our stops didn't result in a search. So, it is a matter, if adding "none" as a value instead of NA will tell a better story here, or, does `search_conducted` as a variable already do the job. Because 98% of our observations don't have a search to go with them, we will append this row as well.

```{r, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(hms)

# Convert stop_time to seconds since midnight
Stops <- Stops %>%
  mutate(
    stop_time_seconds = as.numeric(
      as_hms(stop_time)
    )
  )

# Calculate the mean stop time for each date
daily_means <- Stops %>%
  group_by(stop_date) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_stop_time = mean(
      stop_time_seconds,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Impute missing stop_time values using the daily mean
Stops <- Stops %>%
  left_join(daily_means, by = "stop_date") %>%
  mutate(
    stop_time_seconds = if_else(
      is.na(stop_time_seconds),
      mean_stop_time,
      stop_time_seconds
    ),
    stop_time = as_hms(stop_time_seconds)
  ) %>%
  select(-mean_stop_time, -stop_time_seconds)

# checking our work
sum(is.na(Stops$stop_time))

# Appending `search_type_raw`
Stops <- Stops %>%
  select(-search_type_raw)
```

#### Numeric -\> Categorical & Two Unique Instances

-   `officer_id` is currently a numeric predictor. A model might take a higher `officer_id` as having a greater numeric value as a lower `officer_id`. So, we will convert `officer_id` to a factor.

-   `fine_grained_location` seems to be an instance where the location is different for every stop. We find that we have over 25,000 different exact locations for `fine_grained_location` and the highest count that isn't a missing value or 'same' is 125, or 2.5% of our observations If this is the case, we will remove it as a predictor as well, since se walready have a city and county location. Keeping it would add multicolinearity and make our data sparse in high dimensional space, without giving us predictive power.

    #### Leakage

    -   `is_arrested` as a predictor shares information that is already in our response variable. This is an instance of data leakage. If we use `is_arrested` , information we would only know after the stop, as a predictor, our model will overperform. Thus, we must handle `is_arrested` by removing it from our model.
    -    In the latest case, `stop_outcome` and `stop_duration` would leak data because they are not known until after the stop has been conducted.

```{r, echo = FALSE}

# Converting officer_id to a factor
Stops <- Stops %>%
  mutate(officer_id = as.factor(officer_id))

# Making sure `fine_grained_location` is sparse by checking number of repeat observation in our rows
Stops %>%
  count(fine_grained_location, sort = TRUE)

FGL_counts <- Stops %>%
  count(fine_grained_location, sort = TRUE) %>%
  filter(n > 1)
print(FGL_counts)

Stops <- Stops %>%
  select(-is_arrested, -fine_grained_location, -stop_outcome, -stop_duration)
```

# Correlation of Predictors

To explore relationships among predictors, I created contingency tables and performed chi-square tests of independence for each pair of predictors. The for loop creates a two-way contingency table for each pair pf predictors. These tests helped identify which predictors showed statistically significant associations. All predictor pairs had p-values below 0.05, which suggests that the predictors left after cleaning are associated with one another, which would be expected because the predictors will hopefully correlate to show what the outcome of a traffic stop is.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)

Stops <- Stops %>%
  mutate(
    #Bin time
    time_bin = cut(
      hour(stop_time),
      breaks = seq(0, 24, by = 4),
      labels = c("12AM-4AM", "4AM-8AM", "8AM-12PM",
                 "12PM-4PM", "4PM-8PM", "8PM-12AM"),
      right = FALSE
    ),

    #Bin date into month
    month_bin = month(stop_date, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)
  ) %>%
  select(-stop_time, -stop_date)

results <- data.frame()
#Compare every pair of predictors 
for (i in 1:(ncol(Stops) - 1)) {
  for (j in (i + 1):ncol(Stops)) {

    #Create contingency table
    tbl <- table(Stops[[i]], Stops[[j]])

    #Chi-square test of independence
    test <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tbl))

    #Add results to results table
    results <- rbind(results, data.frame(
      Predictor_1 = names(Stops)[i],
      Predictor_2 = names(Stops)[j],
      Chi_Square = as.numeric(test$statistic),
      P_Value = test$p.value
    ))
  }
}

#Display final table
print(results, row.names = FALSE)

#Conditional counts
table(Stops$driver_race_raw, Stops$search_conducted)
table(Stops$driver_race_raw, Stops$contraband_found)
#Conditional proportions (row percentages)
prop.table(table(Stops$driver_race_raw, Stops$search_conducted), margin = 1)
prop.table(table(Stops$driver_race_raw, Stops$contraband_found), margin = 1)
```

# Graphs of Race, Searches, and Contraband (looking into association)

The first graph shows the probability of a search being conducted based on the driver's race. Black drivers had the highest probability of being searched, followed by Hispanic drivers. White drivers were in the middle for search rate, while Native American and Asian drivers had the lowest search rates. Black drivers were approximately 2.5 times as likely to be searched as White drivers. These differences suggest that there is an association between driver race and whether a search was conducted, which is supported by the chi-square test of independence having a p-value below 0.05.

The second graph shows the probability of contraband being found during a traffic stop based on the driver's race. Hispanic drivers had the highest probability of contraband being found, followed by Black drivers. White drivers had a probability in the middle (about half of what Hispanic and Black drivers had), while Asian drivers had an even lower probability. No contraband was recorded for Native American drivers in the dataset. These results suggest that the probability of contraband being found varies depending on driver race. This relationship is also supported by the chi-square test of independence, which produced a p-value below 0.05.

When comparing the two graphs, Black and Hispanic drivers had the highest search rates and the highest overall contraband=TRUE rates. However, the probability of contraband being found was much lower than the probability of a search being conducted for every racial group, which means most stops don't result in contraband being found.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
#Calculate conditional proportions
search_rates <- Stops %>%
  group_by(driver_race_raw) %>%
  summarise(
    search_rate = mean(search_conducted, na.rm = TRUE) * 100
  )
contraband_rates <- Stops %>%
  group_by(driver_race_raw) %>%
  summarise(
    contraband_rate = mean(contraband_found, na.rm = TRUE) * 100
  )

#Create bar graph
ggplot(search_rates, aes(x = driver_race_raw, y = search_rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "blue") +
  labs(
    title = "Probability of a Search Given Driver Race",
    x = "Driver Race",
    y = "Search Rate (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
ggplot(contraband_rates, aes(x = driver_race_raw, y = contraband_rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "blue") +
  labs(
    title = "Probability of Contraband Found Given Driver Race",
    x = "Driver Race",
    y = "Contraband Found (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
